One of them is the prevention of crime and reducing the fear of crime. Welsh (2008) grouped the explanations of the way street lighting improvements could prevent crime into two main perspectives: first, as a situational crime prevention measure that focuses on reducing opportunity and perceived rewards and increasing perceived risk through modification of the physical environment (Clarke, 1995); and second, as a method of strengthening community confidence, cohesion, and social control through more effective street use (Angel, 1968; Jacobs, 1961) and investment in neighborhood conditions (Kelling, 1996; Skogan, 1990; Wilson, 1982). In fact, improving street lighting has been a popular strategy to prevent crime and to reduce the fear of crime. This reflects a shift towards situational crime prevention using environmental improvements to “design out” opportunities for crime and features that provoke fear (Pain, 2006). As critics argue, it is an approach which bypasses the deeper socioeconomic causes of crime (Gilling, 1997; Koskela and Pain, 2000), but it has had some success in reducing crime and fear in certain areas (Clarke, 1992; Oc and Tiesdell, 1997). Systematic reviews have identified some evidence for improved road safety (Beyer, 2009) and an overall reduction in crime (Welsh, 2008) with increased street lighting. In New York City, temporary streetlights were randomly allocated to public housing developments from March through August 2016. It was found that communities that were assigned more lighting 16 experienced sizable reductions in crime. After accounting for potential spatial spillovers, street lighting reduces outdoor nighttime index crimes by approximately 36% and reduces overall index crimes by approximately 4% in affected communities (Chalfin, et al, 2019). However, with respect to crime, studies show that reductions in victimization are observed during both hours of daylight and darkness (Welsh, 2008), calling into question the mechanism through which improvements to street lighting might influence crime. The research on street lighting illustrates both the possibilities and the problems of the wider situational approach. For the past few decades, experimental programs in the United States and Europe have shown differing results on the effect of street lighting on crime and fear of crime. Among the eight U.S. evaluation studies included in Welsh (2008), results were mixed (Table 4). Four studies found that improved street lighting was effective at reducing crime (Atlanta Regional Commission, 1974; Department of Intergovernmental Fiscal Liaison, 1973; Wright, 1974; Lewis, 1979), while the other four found that it was not effective (Quinet, 1998; Inskeep, 1974; Harrisburg Police Department, 1976; Sternhell, 1977). However, three more studies published in the United Kingdom (Table 5) found significant reductions in crime both in daylight and at nighttime. Table 4.
